Q115590816.summary: This Carolingian ivory casket, with its high gabled lid, is carved on every face with the story of Christ's infancy. On the side shown, the lid presents the Magi, in their Phrygian caps, bringing gifts to the Child, while the panel below shows Herod enthroned among armed guards as he receives the travellers from the East, all set within dense acanthus scrolls. Read around the box, the scenes unfold the mystery of the Incarnation from the Annunciation and Visitation to the Flight into Egypt.
facts: The Louvre attributes the casket to the 'second school of Metz' and dates it to about 870–880 on stylistic grounds.

Besides the Magi before Herod and the Adoration, the Louvre identifies the Dream of Joseph, the Visitation, the angel warning the sleeping Magi, an Annunciation (?), the Flight into Egypt, the Nativity and the Presentation in the Temple on the other faces.
Fixing holes show that a metal mount once covered the edges of the panels; the casket came from the collection of the Lyon painter Pierre Révoil and was bought by the Louvre in 1828.
Q115590816.notes: Inventory MRR 75. Date was given as '870s'; the Louvre gives c. 870–880 and Metz as place of making.
Q115590816.original_title: Coffret : Scènes de l'Enfance du Christ

Q134290568.summary: This small portable altar, with a slab of green porphyry set into its top, is faced with walrus-ivory reliefs crowded with figures beneath towers and arcades. On the side shown, guards lie asleep beside the holy women at the tomb, and at the right Christ, marked by a cross-nimbus, stands among his disciples. Such altars allowed Mass to be celebrated anywhere, with the risen Christ carved around the sacred stone.
facts: Wikidata records scenes of the Crucifixion and the Ascension, the Easter scene at the tomb, and the evangelists on the altar's other faces.
It is about 12.7 cm high and is dated 1050–1075.
Q134290568.notes: Scene identifications for the visible side are made from the photograph (the right-hand scene may be one of Christ's post-Resurrection appearances); the museum's own description was not consulted.

cur:catacombs-daniel-lazarus-relief-vati.summary: Daniel stands naked between two lions, his arms raised in prayer, while at the right Christ, holding a long rod, touches the mummy-like Lazarus standing in a columned tomb on a brick podium. The two deliverances – from the lions and from death – are set side by side as promises of salvation.
facts: Commons places this relief among the Roman sarcophagi of the Museo Pio Cristiano.
The temple-front tomb raised on steps is the standard way of showing Lazarus's grave in Roman art.
cur:catacombs-daniel-lazarus-relief-vati.notes: Inventory number not confirmed; date approximate.

cur:manuscripts-codex-aemilianensis-chri.summary: Within a great lozenge framed by a red and yellow border, Christ stands on a footstool, bearded and haloed, blessing and holding a book, beneath the words 'Alfa et ω' and with 'initium et finis' — 'the beginning and the end' — across the field; cherubim and seraphim occupy the upper corners and the archangels Michael and Gabriel the lower ones. At the foot are the words 'Deus et homo', God and man.
facts: The Codex Aemilianensis is a copy of the Hispana collection of church councils made at San Millán de la Cogolla in 994; its frontispiece closely follows the Codex Vigilanus of 976.
The image is published by the Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial (Patrimonio Nacional) and released under CC0 on Commons.
